itemListElement.name: How to Write a Construction Estimate That Wins Jobs

headline: How to Write a Construction Estimate That Wins Jobs
description: Learn what to include in a construction estimate, how to price line items, set validity dates, and avoid disputes—plus a free template generator.

acceptedAnswer.text: Follow your state and local rules. Many contractors show one tax rate applied to a taxable subtotal and label exempt items such as certain labor or materials. If you are unsure, ask your accountant how to split taxable and non-taxable lines before you send the PDF.

mainEntity.name: What deposit is normal on a remodel?

acceptedAnswer.text: Residential remodels often use twenty-five to forty percent deposits tied to material orders or schedule lock-in. Commercial jobs may use smaller deposits with progress billing. Put the percentage and due date on the estimate so it matches your contract.

mainEntity.name: How detailed should labor hours be?

acceptedAnswer.text: Detailed enough that you can explain the total if challenged, but not so granular that the client micromanages each hour. Phase-level labor lines for rough-in, finish, and punch are a practical middle ground.

mainEntity.name: Can I reuse the same estimate for insurance?

acceptedAnswer.text: Insurance carriers may want photos, codes, and separate material and labor breakdowns. Keep your original estimate and add supplements as change orders rather than editing history silently.

mainEntity.name: When does an estimate become a contract?

acceptedAnswer.text: When both parties sign a written agreement or you accept a deposit with clear terms referencing the estimate. Until then, treat the estimate as an offer that can expire.
